#4319. Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer

For nearly two decades, scientists have known that a common gut bacterium can produce a toxin that damages the colon and helps drive the formation of tumors. What they could not explain was how the toxin first attaches to intestinal cells and begins its attack. Now, researchers have uncovered that missing step, revealing a surprising vulnerability that could lead to new ways of protecting the colon.

The breakthrough comes from a team led by scientists at the Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center, its Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, and the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. Their findings, published in Nature, identify a protein called claudin-4 as the essential docking point for a bacterial toxin known as BFT.

Even more promising, the researchers have already used this discovery to develop a molecular decoy that intercepts the toxin before it can damage colon cells. The strategy successfully protected mice from the toxin's harmful effects, suggesting a possible new approach to preventing bacterial damage associated with colorectal cancer. The research received partial support from the National Institutes of Health.

"We've made several attempts over time to identify the receptor, so this is an exciting moment," says senior author Cynthia Sears, M.D., Bloomberg~Kimmel Professor of Cancer Immunotherapy and professor of medicine at Johns Hopkins. "Understanding how bacterial toxins work can open doors to new approaches for detection and therapy for associated diseases, including diarrhea, colorectal cancer and bloodstream infections."

How a Common Gut Bacterium Can Promote Colon Cancer

The investigation centers on Bacteroides fragilis, a bacterium that can be found in the intestines of up to 20% of healthy people. Although the presence of this bacterium does not automatically mean someone will develop cancer, certain strains produce a powerful toxin capable of disrupting the colon's protective lining, causing inflammation, and encouraging tumor growth.

The toxin, known as B. fragilis toxin or BFT, has been under investigation for years. In a landmark 2009 study published in Nature Medicine, Sears and her colleagues demonstrated that the toxin could promote the development of colon tumors. Their work helped establish an important connection between toxin-producing gut bacteria, chronic inflammation, and colorectal cancer.

Earlier experiments also revealed that BFT damages a protein called E-cadherin, which helps hold neighboring cells together and maintain the colon's protective barrier. When this protein is broken apart, the barrier becomes compromised, potentially allowing harmful substances and bacteria to interfere with the surrounding tissue.

However, one critical question remained unanswered. Although BFT could break down E-cadherin, the toxin did not appear to attach directly to that protein. Researchers suspected that another molecule was helping the toxin reach its target, but repeated attempts to identify it had failed.

Scientists Identify the Missing Link Using CRISPR

To solve the mystery, the researchers turned to CRISPR, a powerful gene-editing technology that allows scientists to selectively disable genes and investigate what they do.

Maxwell White, an M.D./Ph.D. candidate working in Sears' laboratory, led a genome-wide CRISPR screening effort in collaboration with Matthew Waldor's laboratory at Harvard Medical School. The team systematically switched off genes in colon epithelial cells, the cells that form the inner lining of the colon, to determine which ones were necessary for the toxin to attach and cause damage.

One gene stood out dramatically. It produces claudin-4, a protein that helps neighboring cells form tight junctions, the seals that limit the movement of substances between cells and help maintain the intestinal barrier.

When the researchers disabled the gene responsible for claudin-4, BFT could no longer bind to the colon cells. Without that initial attachment, the toxin was unable to attack E-cadherin.

The finding revealed that claudin-4 acts as a receptor for the bacterial toxin. In effect, the toxin must first latch onto this protein before it can carry out its damaging activity.

"It took a while to get the assay working and validate the approach, but once we were able to do the screen, claudin-4 was a clear, resounding top hit," says White. "That was an exciting moment."

An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a New Bacterial Attack Strategy

The identity of the receptor surprised the scientists.

Sears and other researchers had expected BFT to interact with a protein involved in cellular signaling, such as a G protein-coupled receptor. These receptors act somewhat like communication switches, allowing cells to respond to signals from their surroundings.

Claudin-4, however, serves a very different purpose. Rather than functioning primarily as a signaling receptor, it helps maintain the physical connections between neighboring cells.

The discovery also revealed an unusual way for a bacterial toxin to operate. BFT belongs to a class of enzymes called proteases, which cut other proteins. Most proteases act directly on their targets, but BFT appears to require a separate receptor before it can reach and damage E-cadherin.

When the team reviewed previous scientific research, they could not identify another toxin known to use the same mechanism.

To establish that BFT and claudin-4 truly bind to each other, the Johns Hopkins researchers collaborated with structural biologists F. Xavier Gomis-Rüth and Ulrich Eckhard at the Molecular Biology Institute of Barcelona.

Using techniques that measure how molecules interact, White and the Barcelona team showed that BFT and claudin-4 form a tightly bound complex in laboratory experiments. Each toxin molecule paired with one receptor molecule, providing direct physical evidence of the connection.

A Clever Molecular Decoy Blocks the Dangerous Gut Toxin

Identifying the receptor did more than explain how the toxin works. It also gave the scientists an idea for stopping it.

If BFT needs claudin-4 to attach to colon cells, perhaps a substitute could lure the toxin away from its intended target.

To test that possibility, the team developed a molecular decoy. This was a soluble protein carrying sequences from claudin-4, designed to attract BFT without allowing it to attack the colon's protective lining.

The researchers then worked with Min Dong's laboratory at Harvard Medical School, including Kang Wang and colleagues, to investigate the approach in mice. These experiments allowed the scientists to examine how the toxin behaves in the more complicated environment of a living intestine.

The results were encouraging. Instead of binding to claudin-4 receptors on colon cells, BFT attached to the decoy proteins. By intercepting the toxin, the decoys successfully protected the mice from BFT-induced damage.

The finding suggests that it may be possible to interfere with the toxin's first step rather than trying to repair the damage after it occurs.

"This approach could be iterated upon with small molecules or other biologics that have better pharmacological properties," says White. The team is now exploring which molecular approaches might be most successful to block the toxin.

Small molecules are compounds that can sometimes be developed into medicines, while biologics are treatments made from or involving biological materials, such as proteins. Future versions of the decoy strategy could potentially be designed to work more effectively in the body or be easier to administer.

What This Discovery Could Mean for Colon Cancer Prevention

Although the findings identify a promising new target, important questions remain.

Scientists have established that BFT attaches to claudin-4 and that blocking this interaction can protect mice from toxin-induced damage. However, they have not yet captured the exact experimental three-dimensional structure showing how the two molecules fit together.

Even advanced artificial intelligence tools, including AlphaFold, have been unable to fully resolve the interaction. Understanding its precise structure could help researchers design more effective compounds that prevent the toxin from binding.

Further experiments will also be needed to determine whether the decoy approach can safely and effectively prevent toxin-related disease in humans. The mouse experiments demonstrated protection against tissue damage, but they did not establish that the strategy prevents colorectal cancer.

Nevertheless, the discovery resolves a major question that has persisted since the connection between BFT and colon tumor formation was established in 2009. By identifying the toxin's previously unknown point of attachment, researchers have uncovered a potential way to interrupt a harmful biological process before it begins.

The findings could ultimately support new strategies for detecting or treating conditions associated with bacterial toxins, including colorectal cancer, diarrhea, and bloodstream infections.

Additional researchers who contributed to the study include Jason Chen, Shaoguang Wu, Abby L. Geis, and Jessica Queen of Johns Hopkins, along with Hailong Zhang, Karthik Hullahalli, and Jie Zhang of Harvard Medical School.

Funding was provided by the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Janssen Research and Development, Cancer Research UK, the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R01 AI042347, R01 NS080833, R01 NS117626, R01 AI170835 and R01 AI189789) and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.

Materials provided by Johns Hopkins Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4318. NAVI knock world No.1 Spirit out of PGL Masters Bucharest to set up Vitality quarter-final

Team Spirit are out of PGL Masters Bucharest 2026 before the playoffs. Natus Vincere, who knocked them out, now face a Vitality side using stand-in jL.

Team Spirit came into the deciding match as the HLTV.org world number one. The last 2-2 decider of the Swiss stage, against Natus Vincere, ended their event.

The match swung sharply. NAVI dominated the opening map on Cache. Spirit pulled level on Dust2, but it was NAVI who closed the series out on Anubis. HLTV reported that it was Spirit’s first defeat by NAVI since February 2025.

NAVI’s run to the playoffs was uneven. They opened with 2-0 wins over G2 and FURIA, and the second map against G2 went to three overtimes. Then the form dipped.

BetBoom beat them 2-0, on Dust II 10-13 and Nuke 9-13. Vitality followed, with NAVI losing Inferno 2-13 and Dust II 9-13. That second straight defeat dropped NAVI into the 2-2 pool, where one more loss would have ended their event.

Spirit took a similar route to the decider. They lost 1-2 to MOUZ on 27 October. Spirit won Nuke 13-2 but then lost Dust2 8-13 and Mirage 14-16.

Elimination at 2-3 has a clear financial cost. Teams finishing ninth to eleventh each receive US$31,250. Each losing quarter-finalist takes US$50,000. The winners’ share is split equally between players and organisation.

NAVI were not the only late qualifiers. Nemiga beat The MongolZ 2-0 and FURIA beat Liquid 2-0 on the final group-stage day. Those three teams took the last three playoff places.

The rematch comes quickly, against the Vitality side that beat NAVI in the group stage. The other ties are Nemiga v FUT, Aurora v MOUZ and BetBoom v FURIA.

Vitality are not at full strength. The organisation announced in August that Justinas ‘jL’ Lekavicius would stand in at BLAST Open Porto and PGL Masters Bucharest.

The stakes extend beyond this event. NAVI’s tournament page calls Bucharest the penultimate major tournament before the PGL Major Singapore 2026. A deep run here would give any of the eight teams momentum heading into that event.

WE ARE IN THE PGL MASTERS BUCHAREST 2026 PLAYOFFS! #navination pic.twitter.com/rdiI6PbxUr

PGL Masters Bucharest is an offline S-Tier event, rated Valve Tier 1, featuring 16 teams. The playoffs use a single-elimination bracket and include a separate match for third place. There is no second chance for anyone from here.

#4317. Ace Combat 8: Wings Of Theve Review – Soaring Higher Than Ever

Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve flies on the tailwinds of its predecessor, which brought life back to the series in 2019. Yet it also dips deep into the series' wealth of mechanics and themes – wingmen, huge mission areas, memorable rivals – to forge what feels like the ace of aces, and one of the series' best entries.

In the wake of an invasion of your homeland, you go down in a dogfight with Sotoa's elite Shadow squadron alongside the "Wings of Theve," a folk hero for the FCU that you discover is a little more tall tale than living legend. You don his identity and become the new "Wings of Theve" to help keep the war effort alive.

Though Ace Combat is certainly no stranger to stories about war, politics, and their effect on the world at large, Wings of Theve takes it to a new height thanks to its focus on your wingmen and the crew of your carrier, the Endurance. Over 30 missions, you build a small band of surviving fighters aboard your meager fleet, all hoping to make it to the conflict's resolution. From your Joker Squadron and sister Queen Squadron to enemy aces and crew aboard the Endurance, the cast is both packed and memorable.

Though there are still some odd story wrinkles, specifically when asking for an arbitrary button press to advance the scene, and the voice of the former Wings pilot Cope speaking to you from the beyond lays on a little thick at the start, Ace Combat 8's story soars thanks to its new first-person perspective and focus on the squadron around you and other members of the Endurance. Big moments in missions hit that much harder when you've spent time around these pilots, seen their struggles up close, and then have to desperately battle alongside them for your life in the skies above.

Each mission is a brilliantly laid-out box of objectives and tasks, an impressive feat given the variety of what Bandai's Aces team asks you to accomplish. In one, you soar across a vast desert, taking out strategic reserves of power, ammo, and hangars full of planes to whittle down an invasion force's resources. In another, you jet toward an island at high speeds and low altitudes to avoid radar detection; then, several missions later, you're trailing massive cargo planes in the sky, following their contrails because radar jamming masks their exact position.

A wealth of planes and weapons are available, and all feel fantastic to fly. The jets feel a little heavier than in Ace Combat 7, but it's a good heft; in the midst of a high-G turn, it appropriately feels like you're wresting the nose of a giant mass of steel at sonic speeds. You can also pack two special weapons at a time, which lets you specialize more and opens up more options in your hangar for each outing. I still found myself beelining straight for the F-35C, but enjoyed several of the other options as well; one special section involving an A-10 bomber was a particularly fun break from the whiplash-inducing missile rodeo of other missions.

It's not just missiles the enemy will throw at you, either. Get used to hearing "Rail Gun Warning" in your headphones, as Sotoa's fleet of land battleships and other terra-naval units make ground forces especially troublesome in Ace Combat 8. Sotoa's Lux Lunae, or the Shadows as your squad calls them, are also a highlight. From their sleek black paint jobs and open-comms chanting as they enter the battlefield to their mid-air maneuvers, the Shadows continually push you to the edge and beyond. Besting the Lux Lunae's aces was a consistent source of improvement and achievement as a virtual pilot.

Multiplayer pushes even further, with modes for those who just like to chase high scores and those who want to dogfight other human pilots. Modes where your four-flier squad compete for score, either alongside or against an enemy squadron, make up the bulk of multiplayer playtime. The star attraction is the emergency sorties: special missions that fire up every so often for all players, pitting them against Ace Combat superweapons like the Arsenal Bird. It's a solid base with room to grow for future support, though a lot of menuing, grinding for specific plane upgrade needs, and cosmetic monetization options put speed bumps on my playtime more often than I'd have liked.

Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve perfectly represents why fliers have stuck with this series. A fantastic campaign, filled with missions I want to replay over and over again, is buoyed by a compelling cast and story, excellent flight controls, explosive dogfights, and encounters you can't wait to scream through at supersonic speeds. Ace Combat 8 proves the series is no museum piece; Wings of Theve soars with the best of the best, and it's a blast to play again and again.

#4316. Etheria Restart tier list and a reroll guide

You won't be able to craft the best team if you don't know who the finest characters are in the game, and that's where our Etheria Restart tier list steps in.

Updated on November 2nd, 2026 - Version: 2.0.2 - Added: Dawnlight Nell

Since ER is a gacha, you probably already know that if you aim to be among the best players on your server, you need to have a specific team that can easily clear out the stages. The characters in the S tier are the ones you should aim to get, either by rerolling or by getting lucky with your pulls.

So far, we've shared the latest Etheria Restart codes, which also give you some free summoning tickets (Anima Prototypes). Make sure to claim these before they expire, and then read through this guide.

Etheria Restart character ranking breakdown At the top of the Etheria Restart tier list, we have characters that excel at their specific role - be it healers or supports, which will help your team stay alive during difficult battles, such as Freya, or outstanding DPS characters, such as Massiah, who is a beast in terms of damage dealt.

Of course, there are more than just these two I mentioned, so when you think about putting together a team, you need to take into account what enemy you're up against and what your team needs specifically (sustain, more damage, or dispelling buffs from the enemy, for example).

The synergy among these characters is also important, but if you manage to pull two or three of the characters listed in the S+ tier and use them, you'll be good to go. Once upgraded, they will help you clear out all the stages easily.

So, without further ado, let's check out who those characters are and dive into our this tier list! S+ tier  |  S tier  |  A tier  |  B tier  |  C tier

Reroll guide Original article by Cristina Mesesan. Updated by Mihail Katsoris.

Massiah is one of the best DPS characters you can currently get in Etheria: Restart. His Divine Descent grants him Invincibility for a turn, which can be massive, especially in PvE. His Defiance Cross can also grant that, or extend his existing Invincibility for a turn - it can give you a massive advantage if used correctly. His PvP prowess is also good, since he can ignore DEF, making him great for any team. Freya is one of the characters that everyone should aim to get, since her support kit is downright broken. She can grant buffs, such as increasing allies' turn meter (which means your allies can spam skills), but she can also debuff enemies in the same way. On top of that, she can grant the Nightmare effect, which helps allies heal themselves when they attack an enemy with that effect. Lingluo is another top-tier support who revolves mainly around heals. While she has pretty low defences by default, her heals more than make up for it. With all of the skills in her kit, she heals allies, but some of them, such as Whirlpool, can also dispel debuffs. Her whole kit is about buffs, debuffs, or enhancing existing buffs, which works great with most of the other characters in this tier.

Rahu is a great DPS/Support character, but the main reason he is not at the top of our Etheria Restart tier list is that he's kinda hard to master. You need to time his kit perfectly to support allies or enhance his damage, which can be tricky at times. When mastered, Rahu can be quite insane, especially as a single-target DPS. Otherwise, he can be fairly average. He mainly shines in PvP, where he excels at shielding. Beyontin is an SSR support, and one of the very few characters that actually has a revive in her kit. Not only that, she can also buff allies' turn meter with her Bloom Sonata AND with her Soul Whirl. With her Karma Abyss, she can buff allies' ATK and Crit DMG for 2 turns, which makes her one of the best supports in Etheria: Restart. Gray is just an SR, and one that you get from the tutorial. However, he is extremely strong as a debuffer, which means you can use him from the moment you get him. He can also buff his turn meter, and with his kit, he can also buff his and his allies' Crit rate, meaning he's a great addition to any team.

Borgne is an SSR DPS character who is able to do amazing AoE damage. He is a fairly straightforward damage dealer, one who has pretty good sustain in his kit, but because he doesn't really scale with Crits, he is only placed in this tier. Veronika is a decent character for PvE, but she excels at PvP. She is quite hit or miss, depending on your luck, but for PvP, she is one of the best. Her kit is designed to "steal" buffs from enemies and spread them amongst her teammates, which is why she's more of a situational character (the situation here being PvP). Chiaki is a decent healer, and an SR one too. She is fairly straightforward, her entire kit focusing mostly on healing her team. If you don't have any better healers, she can do a pretty reliable job.

Rilmocha is a decent DPS character, mainly used in specific situations. She has good AoE, but is not the best in terms of single-target damage. She relies a lot on splash damage (damage dealt to nearby enemies when attacking an enemy), which can be good AoE. Cachi the Guard is an SR character you get during the tutorial - he is a decent debuffer, but nothing really mind-blowing. He can decrease the enemy's Crit Rate and Speed. Dorothy is a character you will get during the tutorial, and she is pretty middle-of-the-pack. She's a decent and fairly straightforward healer. She is not great, but not horrible either. Let's just say she is okay until you get something better.

Sybil, the one character you get from the tutorial. I don't recommend upgrading any of them, since they won't be of much use, or any use at all, for that matter.

#4315. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

#4314. New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss

An experimental electronic implant could offer an entirely new way to treat type 2 diabetes. Rather than relying on insulin or conventional medications, the device uses electricity to convert excess blood sugar into a substance that the body can eliminate. In early tests with diabetic mice, the technology successfully regulated blood sugar and also led to weight loss.

The development comes as type 2 diabetes continues to affect a growing number of people worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, type 2 is frequently associated with obesity, limited physical activity, and consuming more energy than the body needs over long periods.

Insulin injections can help reduce blood sugar by allowing muscle cells to absorb glucose from the bloodstream. However, insulin does not eliminate the underlying problem of excess energy. When the body does not use the glucose it absorbs, the surplus can eventually be converted into fat. This helps explain why some people with diabetes continue gaining weight even while receiving treatment.

Researchers led by Martin Fussenegger, a professor in the Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering at ETH Zurich in Basel, have developed an implant designed to address this problem differently. Their findings were published in the journal Science.

A New Diabetes Treatment Powered by Electricity

Fussenegger and his colleagues have spent years developing technologies capable of controlling blood sugar. Their previous designs used engineered genetic networks, but these systems depended on living cells and other biological materials.

That dependence introduced several complications. Biological components can create challenges involving immune compatibility, long-term stability, production, and regulatory approval.

The researchers have now taken a different approach by creating a catalyst made entirely from inorganic materials. It performs its function without requiring living cells, enzymes, or other biological components.

At the heart of the implant is a piece of graphite felt covered with tiny clusters of gold. These gold structures are coated with even smaller platinum particles, creating a specially engineered surface that enables the chemical reaction needed to process glucose.

The researchers designed this nanoscale surface themselves. According to Fussenegger, the materials also demonstrated excellent biocompatibility during experimental testing, suggesting they can interact with living tissue without causing significant adverse reactions.

The system includes an electronic controller enclosed in a 3D-printed housing. Instead of relying on a conventional wired power connection, the implant receives energy wirelessly at a frequency of 13.56 MHz. This frequency is internationally allocated for industrial, scientific, and medical applications.

How the Implant Removes Excess Blood Sugar

The technology works by transforming excess glucose into gluconate, a substance that can be eliminated from the body through urine.

Normally, glucose provides energy for cells. When more glucose is available than the body needs, some of that excess energy can ultimately be stored as fat. By converting part of the glucose into gluconate, the implant prevents that portion from being metabolized and stored in tissues, potentially helping reduce fat accumulation.

The entire process is designed to happen automatically, responding to changes in blood sugar as they occur.

A conventional glucose sensor, similar to those worn on the upper arm by many people with diabetes, continuously measures glucose concentrations in tissue. When levels rise too high, such as after a meal, the sensor communicates through Bluetooth with a smartphone or smartwatch.

The connected device then activates the implant, supplying the electrical energy needed for the catalyst to convert glucose into gluconate.

Once glucose levels return to the desired range, the implant automatically shuts down. This feedback system, known as closed-loop control, is intended to prevent blood sugar from dropping dangerously low.

Blood Sugar Control and Weight Loss in Diabetic Mice

To evaluate the technology, the researchers first conducted a laboratory experiment using a reservoir containing 5 liters of a nutrient solution with glucose. That volume is approximately equal to the amount of blood circulating in an adult human body.

The experiment demonstrated that the catalyst could convert glucose in a solution of this scale, an important step toward assessing its potential for medical applications.

The researchers then implanted the system in diabetic mice. The results showed that the device could precisely regulate the animals' blood sugar levels. The mice also lost weight, suggesting that converting excess glucose rather than allowing it to contribute to fat storage could offer an additional metabolic benefit.

Over six weeks of testing, the implant continued functioning reliably and was well tolerated by the animals.

"The system operates at a very low voltage, and our experiments showed no evidence of tissue damage from either electrical or thermal effects," says Fussenegger.

Although these findings are promising, the device has not yet been tested in humans. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the technology can operate safely and effectively in people with diabetes.

Could Electronics Transform the Future of Diabetes Treatment?

Fussenegger believes the technology could represent a fundamental change in how diabetes is managed. Rather than using medications to influence how the body processes glucose, an electronic device could directly control the amount of glucose available.

"For decades, we have treated diabetes by telling the body how to manage glucose. We are now showing that we can take control of glucose directly, using electronics rather than drugs," he says. "And the catalyst only activates when glucose levels are too high."

The approach also creates opportunities to connect medical treatments with digital technologies, including the Internet of Things. This refers to networks of devices that exchange information and respond automatically to changing conditions.

The researchers envision electronically controlled treatments that could be manufactured at scale and integrated with existing digital health systems.

Their next objective is to turn the experimental implant into a medical device suitable for further development and eventual clinical testing.

One potential advantage is its relatively simple glucose conversion mechanism. Because the catalyst does not rely on cells or enzymes, the researchers believe some of the technical challenges associated with biological treatments could be easier to overcome.

Much of the supporting technology is also already available. Wireless power transmission systems and external electronic controllers are commercially established, meaning the team would not need to develop every component from scratch.

If future studies demonstrate similar benefits in humans, this approach could open the door to a new class of diabetes treatments in which smart electronic devices help regulate blood sugar directly, potentially reducing reliance on conventional medications.

Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4312. The best soft launch mobile games for iPhone, iPad or Android

The biggest games yet to launch on the global market

If you've been looking for something new and exciting that isn't quite fully released, then look no further; you've found our list of the best games currently in soft launch.

Sometimes developers like to make sure the paying public is willing to play their game before they push it to every device in the world - that's where soft launch comes in. Available in just a handful of countries and regions, a soft-launched game is subject to drastic change as developers take on board customer feedback (and other metrics) to alter the game and ensure the best possible product is ready for when it goes to worldwide launch.

But here's the kicker - we can see when developers do that. And when you're looking at some of the big games, like the ones we have on this list, then you can find yourself getting very excited, and even a little jealous that you can't play them yet.

So to help you out a little, we've collected a huge list of some of the biggest and best games currently available in soft launch, which you might well be able to get if you have the right Apple ID or Google Play account to download them with.

Just as a note: In the case of a game suddenly disappearing, it might be because the developer has decided to stop development on it early and save themselves the cost of a big launch, or because the developer is gearing up for a big launch and wants to surprise the world. Whatever the case, we'll try to keep you updated when these things happen.

Let's get into the list! Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble

Insomniac's beloved duo are back on mobile. Well, sort of. While you can only play the titular pair during certain events, the essence of Ratchet & Clank is very much here. Across several game modes, you'll duke it out with other players using all the delightfully wacky weapons from the series' history.

An interesting one here. Bandai Namco has dived back into the mobile world with a completely new IP. They're also claiming it's the first 'Match3D Roguelite Battle Game ever.' Given the sheer breadth of games out there, I highly doubt it, but it's an intriguing combination, nonetheless.

Sonic Rumble sees the blue blur returning to mobile, this time as a battle royale of sorts. In the mould of games like Stumble Guys and Fall Guys, it appears we can expect to dash around obstacle-filled courses, dodging the numerous hazards that threaten to eliminate us at every turn. It's definitely a setup that suits Sonic and co, but is it entering a market that's already been conquered by Scopely? Only time will tell.

Casual strategy games are all the rage these days, particularly on mobile. Anything that gives you a slight hit of feeling clever without requiring in-depth tactics that take forever to learn. Century Games' Crown of Bones is the latest attempt at sliding into that niche. It sees you joining the Skeleton King and his army as they battle through numerous realms. It sports a colourful art style that reminds me somewhat of little toy towns and villages, something you might have created in real life as a child, perhaps. As for the gameplay, it pretty much consists of increasing your numbers, upgrading your troops and toppling your opponents. There are a few special items thrown in for good measure as well.

If you're a football fan, you're probably already aware of Nordeus as the folks behind the popular management sim Top Eleven. With their latest effort, Top Goal, they are swapping the touchline for the pitch as you take direct control over your squad, having a more active role in the outcome of a match. Still, it seems some of the strategic side remains as you build your squad and choose your formation before taking on other players in PvP.

While it might seem as though the era of endless runners has passed on mobile, several still do very well, particularly if they have brand power behind them. Zapak hopes that Ben 10 Alien Run can join that list, putting a lot of stock in the popular children's cartoon pulling in the younger generation.

In it, you will dash around while transforming into one of nine different aliens, each bringing special abilities to the table. That might be creating a shield to block an enemy attack in one instance, while another might clear the path ahead with laser beams. On top of that, there are the usual daily challenges and missions you'd expect from the genre.

Oh My Anne is a match-3 game based on the popular novel series Anne of Green Gables. Players proceed through the story by completing levels and associated challenges. It's certainly interesting to see Neowiz deciding to take established, historical (1908~) novels and their IP and spin them off into games. There's a question to be asked about brand recognition and 'crossover IP' when those IPs are not ones from the current vogue. We regularly see Warhammer and Marvel crossover games, but those things are currently 'in', Anne of Green Gables — and Oh My Anne — targets a different audience and plays by different rules of advertising. Could there be a Dracula, Canterbury Tales or Beowulf games on the horizon if this takes off?

NetEase's Stumble Guys killer, Eggy Party, is rapidly moving toward its global release with seven new regions granted access to it in January of 2024; before that, it was simply in the SEA region. What's the big appeal? Well, if you're not sold by the constant party, cheerful colours and multiplayer mania of Eggy Party, then maybe the map creation will be the thing to grab your attention. A bumbling race to the finish might be fun, but doing it on a map that you - or one of your friends - created is vastly more fun.

Zynga, who you likely know for, well, many things, are working on a new addition to their growing merge catalogue. FruitFall – don't forget the double capital Fs – tasks you with merging fruits to beat each level. Simple, right? Judging by the store description, expect this to become more difficult as you progress. At first, it'll likely be a case of simply merging fruit, while the latter stages will introduce troublesome crates and frozen fruit that need thawing out before becoming useful. Zynga claims each level brings something different, keeping the challenge fresh and fun. Time will tell if that's the case

Mattel Match: Toybox looks to bring together the company's many toys under one roof, including Uno, Masters of the Universe and, of course, Barbie. How? You might ask. Through match-3 puzzling, that's how.

As you'll likely have guessed from the name, Puzzletown Mysteries sees you unravel mysteries by solving puzzles. There is also a town involved. The overarching whodunit is whether poor Gladys slipped from her balcony or if she received a little push before toppling over the edge, while you'll also look into a case of stolen cats.

As you've likely already guessed from the name, we're talking tower defence here. Here, the slight twist on the usual formula is that, alongside setting up your various defences, you'll actually build the map your enemies will march down. Of course, that's something we've seen before, but it's a fun twist nevertheless. I'm quite fond of the visuals, which have a super clean and easy-to-read look that's just shy of qualifying as minimalist.

Diamond Dreams is looking to bring a sense of elegance to the match-3 genre. The whole idea is that you're working towards crafting some stunning jewellery that, I have to say, looks far better than it possibly needs to.

Given the immense popularity of Monopoly Go, it seemed inevitable that similar games would pop up eventually. Coin Master – Board Adventure from Moon Active is one such attempt. Having already achieved success with Coin Master, I'd imagine this will also do incredibly well.

Cats & Soup has made a name for itself in recent times with its lovely aesthetic and focus on feline companions. While it's still a fairly familiar idle RPG, the focus on cosiness helped it stand out from a massive crowd. Evidently buoyed by its success, a spin-off called Cats & Soup: Magic Recipe is now in the works. Once again, the team are taking on a familiar mobile genre, bringing some warm-fuzzy cuteness to the merge-and-match realm. The aim is to cook delicious recipes, build a lovely home for your kitties, and make friends with new cats.

The humble match-3 will likely never lose popularity on mobile. It's simple to understand and great for playing on the go since it hits a nice spot between relaxing and engaging the brain. It's not surprising, then, that we often have big franchises delve into the genre. The latest to try their white-gloved hand is Disney with Disney Magic Match 3D. In it, you'll remove colourful clutter. No, really. Check out Catherine's preview to learn more.

While George R R Martin might have no interest in finishing his own book series, there is still plenty of Game of Thrones content to enjoy. Dragonfire is the latest, a tile-based strategy game that lets you put the titular fire-breathing winged beasties to work. But it's not simply sending them into battle. You will hatch and train them, taking your little fiery friend from a cute baby to a creature capable of barbecuing enemy villages.

We all love Fruit Ninja, but if there's one criticism you can throw its way, it's that it didn't have much else going for it beyond slicing up fruit. Adventure looks to change this by introducing a level-based approach that sees you solving puzzles alongside stabbing melons. You can also unlock new weapons and abilities as you progress, presumably allowing you to dice a kiwi in untold ways.

FairyTale Quest is a roguelite action RPG in the style of something like Vampire Survivors. And its characters? Well, as you've likely guessed, they're all pulled from traditional stories. So you can expect the Big Bad Wolf and Red Riding Hood to fight by your side. They can put aside their differences for the greater good, it seems.

That's right. Plants Vs Zombies 3 is back in soft launch, this time with Evolved after the colon. This refers to the merging mechanics they're throwing in with their latest attempt. We'll see how that all pans out in due course, but it's hard not to be a little sceptical given that EA has clearly struggled to figure out what they want to do with PvZ.

It's been almost ten years since Hill Climb Racing 2 launched, so it likely feels about time for a sequel for fans of wacky, physics-based driving. In the third instalment, you can expect plenty of special gadgets and handy boosts for increasing your performance on the bouncy track. There are also the plentiful customisation options on offer that any self-respecting racer needs. If we can't pimp our ride, what's the point?

Aside from the obvious flock and little green candy-loving monster, there are few games more iconic on mobile than Temple Run. That's why the announcement of a third has got us excited here at Pocket Gamer. But do those simple yet effective mechanics stand up after all these years, or are massive changes needed? Well, check out Catherine's Temple Run 3 preview to see what she thought.

Cute little penguins running around an obstacle course in Fall/Stumble Guys fashion? Haven't we already seen this with Pudgy Party? Apparently, Smilegate thinks they can do better, and personally, I'm all for it. Penguins are wonderful little creatures, and the more games where they're the star, the better. It sees you participating in 10-minute matches where the aim is to get your beak across the line first.

If you love pinging marbles and cutesy creatures, Marblebound might be the perfect fit for you. You gather a team of four heroes and then head into battle to take down a series of fearsome foes. And you'll do that by firing marbles at them, including ricocheting them off walls if you know your angles.

FunPlus, who you may know from State of Survival and DC: Dark Legion, among others, appears to be working on a new game. This one's called Dark Shot Survival and sees you building up a base to fend off night creatures (yes, they look like zombies to me, too). The whole thing seems to centre around a day/night cycle, wherein you spend the waking hours gathering resources and fortifying your base. Then, when the sun goes down, you'll need to fend off the zomb— sorry, night creatures, with all your might.

Angry Birds Rush sees Rovio's recognisable avians slinging themselves into a different genre. By the looks of things, Rush is an endless runner that sees you bouncing through various colourful locales all inspired by the series' many other games. It doesn't appear to be a straightforward runner, though, with slingshot elements still present to some extent.

There are few cartoon duos more iconic than Tom & Jerry. I'm not even a huge fan of them, but they'd certainly spring to mind if I had to name two long-standing cartoon rivals. It's that instant recognition that probably helped Steer Studios decide it was an IP worth working with. Tom and Jerry Blast is a puzzler that, based on the screenshots, sees you tapping your way through each level and using boosters if they ever become overly tricky.

You wouldn't necessarily put sailing the seven seas and tower defence together, but that's exactly what Puzala is going for with Stormborn Era. In it, you take charge of Black Sam and his crew, defending their ship from the hordes of enemies that have nothing better to do with their time than attack a big boat.

The Girls' Frontline series has proven incredibly popular over the years. Apparently, conventionally attractive women with guns will always do well. Who knew? Anyway, you can check out Catherine's Ahead of the Game to see if it's more than just a surface-level shooter.

Having briefly appeared in the US a while back, Borderlands Mobile has crept back into soft launch in Canada. The latest iteration has revealed that we can play as long-time fan-favourite Mad Moxxi, which I'm sure will be welcome news to many folks.

#4311. Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep

A major new scientific review is raising questions about whether medical cannabis actually helps people with insomnia. Despite growing interest in cannabis as a sleep treatment, researchers found that the available evidence is too weak to reliably determine whether it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or how well people function during the day.

Insomnia affects millions of people and can make it difficult to fall asleep, remain asleep throughout the night, or wake up feeling rested. Beyond the frustration of sleepless nights, the condition can seriously disrupt daily life and increase the likelihood of developing anxiety or depression.

Treatments for insomnia include cognitive behavioral therapy, which helps people change thoughts and habits that interfere with sleep, as well as medications such as antidepressants and antipsychotics. However, these approaches do not work equally well for everyone, fueling interest in alternative options.

Medical cannabis has attracted particular attention because of its potential to improve sleep. Unlike recreational cannabis, regulated medical products typically contain carefully measured amounts of THC and CBD, two compounds found in cannabis, and are administered as tablets, sprays, or oils. Despite its growing popularity, scientists have continued to debate whether cannabis offers meaningful benefits for people with insomnia.

Major Review Finds Little Evidence of Sleep Benefits

To investigate, researchers from The Cochrane Associate Centre at the Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires and the University of Manitoba examined nine clinical studies involving 537 adults between the ages of 18 and 76 who were receiving treatment for insomnia.

Most of the studies involved people with primary insomnia, meaning their sleep problems were not attributed to another medical condition. Eight trials compared regulated medical cannabis with a placebo, an inactive treatment used to measure whether a therapy produces genuine benefits. The remaining trial compared cannabis with amitriptyline, an antidepressant that is sometimes used to treat sleep problems.

Across the placebo comparisons, medical cannabis produced little or no clinically meaningful improvement in sleep quality, satisfaction with sleep, total hours slept, or daytime functioning.

The researchers also identified potential drawbacks. Participants who received medical cannabis were substantially more likely to experience mild side effects, including dizziness and dry mouth, than those given a placebo. However, this finding came from a relatively small number of studies, limiting confidence in the result.

There was some indication that medical cannabis might improve overall quality of life. Yet the evidence supporting this possibility was highly uncertain. When the findings were combined, the results were consistent with outcomes ranging from a slight decline in quality of life to a substantial improvement.

"The main message is that the research currently available is not sufficient to reliably answer whether medical cannabis helps people with insomnia," says Dr. Lucia Varela, lead author of the study from the University of Manitoba, Canada. "This does not mean that medical cannabis is ineffective. It means that, based on the evidence we have, we cannot draw reliable conclusions about its effectiveness for insomnia in the general population."

Why Scientists Remain Uncertain About Cannabis and Insomnia

One of the biggest problems was the quality of the research itself. The reviewers rated their confidence in the available evidence as low or very low, citing small study populations, conflicting findings, and potential bias in how the trials were conducted.

Another challenge was the lack of consistency between studies. Researchers tested different medical cannabis products, making it difficult to directly compare their results or determine whether particular formulations might work better than others.

The studies were also relatively short. The longest followed participants for just 12 weeks, leaving major unanswered questions about whether medical cannabis could provide lasting sleep benefits or produce additional effects with prolonged use.

More Research Is Needed Before Cannabis Can Be Recommended

The researchers also cautioned that the study participants did not adequately represent the broader population of people living with insomnia.

Women accounted for nearly three-quarters (72.66% of participants), and the research was heavily weighted toward younger adults. As a result, it remains unclear whether the findings would apply equally to men, older individuals, or people whose insomnia occurs alongside other medical conditions.

Taken together, these limitations mean that the existing research cannot establish whether medical cannabis is an effective insomnia treatment. The authors emphasize that larger, more rigorous clinical trials are needed before it can be confidently recommended for improving sleep.

Importantly, the findings do not establish that medical cannabis is ineffective. Instead, they highlight how much remains unknown about a treatment that has gained considerable attention despite limited high-quality evidence.

"The evidence is too weak and uncertain to draw firm conclusions about the use of medical cannabis for insomnia," says Dr. Luis Garegnani, senior author from Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires, Argentina. "Rather than viewing the findings as either an endorsement or a rejection of medical cannabis, clinicians and patients should recognize the uncertainty and consider individual circumstances while better evidence is generated."

Materials provided by Cochrane. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
