#4251. 8 Best JRPGs Without an Open World

Melissa Sarnowski is a Gaming Writer at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2022. She specializes in lists, reviews, and features, with additional experience writing guides for Hardcore Gamer.

I love exploring open worlds, but that doesn't mean that I want every game I play to feature one. JRPGs are one of the genres where you find a mix of map styles, letting you decide the style you want at that time as you search for a game to play.

These games are for those who love JRPGs but don't want to spend months on the same playthrough.

An open world can be fun in that it makes the in-game universe feel expansive and alive. At the same time, having extra content might become tedious if you like to do completionist runs, or you can end up entirely distracted by side quests, ignoring the main quests. Without an open world, you can focus on the narrative and characters, keeping the spotlight on them rather than their world.

When the topic of JRPGs comes up, Chrono Trigger usually gets mentioned, too. This might be one of the most classic and beloved JRPGs, and its mechanics trick you into feeling like the world is more expansive than the areas you can access.

Time traveling in Chrono Trigger lets you pick different eras and locations in those eras to send your party, giving you the illusion of a large world without making it an open world. It's almost crazy how a map can feel large and detailed without letting you freely explore it.

Across the series, Persona has so much content to offer that having an open world on top of that would simply be excessive. The Persona games blend classic features of JRPGs, such as turn-based combat, with elements that you’d normally find in social simulators to give you a unique and immersive experience.

Persona 3, in particular, has just been remade as Persona 3 Reload, although the female protagonist from the original wasn’t included this time. Still, it’s been given a modern polish, making it a great time to try Persona 3 if you haven’t played it before and want a break from open-world games.

Another game that’s in the middle of being remade is Trails in the Sky, which you might’ve seen as Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter, with the 2nd Chapter having been released recently. The Third Chapter has not yet been released, or even confirmed. The games are part of the larger The Legend of Heroes series, but Trails in the Sky is a perfect piece that you can play without knowledge of the overall series.

Trails in the Sky gives you the classic JRPG experience that’s so gripping you don’t notice that it’s not an open world. You have the protagonists chasing their dreams of being senior Bracers, but they end up in the middle of a larger, more dangerous conspiracy that they didn’t know was threatening their home.

In the mood for more sci-fi in your JRPG? While many JRPGs like to lean into more traditional fantasy settings or a blend of fantasy and sci-fi, Cosmic Star Heroine dives fully into sci-fi and takes you into space in a 16-bit style reminiscent of classic 90s JRPGs.

I love the story of Cosmic Star Heroine, and space-based and heavy cyberpunk-themed games usually aren’t fully open-world anyway because, well, that’s a big task. Still, you get to be a secret agent for the Agency of Peace and save the entire galaxy. How cool is that?

You might not think it from the title, but Lunar: Silver Star Story Complete is kind of a story about dragons. Well, it’s a story about dragonmasters, specifically, which is still a pretty cool title to have. As you expect from older games, since it was released in North America in 1999, it doesn’t have an open world, but gives you the feeling that you get to explore a sizable area anyway.

Lunar: Silver Star Story Complete has you band together with your friends to become the next true dragonmaster, and the story combined with the animated cutscenes creates an overall charming experience.

Final Fantasy in general tends to favor more linear maps, but that's not necessarily true for every entry. Some fall more into a semi-open-world style, and others have at least a section that's open world, if not more. As for which game to play among the many options, Final Fantasy 10 is always a solid choice.

These are games for those who want to dig deeper into the genre.

FF10 has puzzle areas that can feel more open, although they're still quite constrained, but the overall focus is the narrative and characters. The world is an important backdrop, but the game isn't going to let you get lost in it and avoid the main objectives.

Remade in 2024, the Switch version of Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door adds more features and a lot of polish, but it keeps the story untouched. I feel like Paper Mario tends to get overlooked when JRPGs are the topic of conversation, but the games are so charming.

On top of being charming, they’re automatically familiar because it’s difficult to not be familiar with Mario when you’re in the gaming space. Then, you have some added silliness with the abilities Mario has as paper, which are just fun to play with.

Perhaps the Holy Grail of JRPGs, Grandia is about as classic of an experience as you can get. It even makes the world feel massive without it being an open-world map, which is rather incredible. There’s also an HD version of the Grandia games that gives you some modern quality-of-life features that are always nice.

The story also doesn’t get more classic than this. You want to be an adventurer like your father, and fate seems to support this when you inherit a spirit stone and begin a journey with your friends to save the world and uncover mysteries.

JRPG worlds just kept getting bigger and deeper in the seventh console generation, and especially on the PS3.

#4250. Google Ocarina Of Time To Transport Your Browser Back To 1998

Hard to believe, but it’s almost Ocarina of Time remake release day. Launching exclusively on Switch 2 on November 5, we are now just days away from experiencing a remake of what many consider to be the greatest game ever made, and Google has kicked off the celebrations early with a rather unique Legend of Zelda easter egg.

If you enter Ocarina of Time on Google and hit enter, which I imagine many of you will be doing a lot this week, whether it be to watch all of the remake’s trailers one last time or check in on your pre-order, there should be a Master Sword in the bottom right of your screen.

Click it, and your screen will be hit with the same blue and white effect that surrounds Link when he pulls the Master Sword in the original game, with a golden Triforce in the center. Once the effect fades, you’ll still be looking at the search results for Ocarina of Time; it’ll just look like you’re viewing them through a 1998 lens.

That’s because the Zelda easter egg in question is a time-traveling one that, when used, makes your search results look the way that they did when the original Ocarina of Time was released in 1998. The Google logo has reverted to the way it appeared back then, complete with its long-forgotten exclamation mark, and the “Google Search” and “I’m Feeling Lucky” buttons are the big, grey chunky ones synonymous with ‘90s Windows that really felt like you were doing something when you clicked them.

The search results themselves are a lot more basic. Cleaner and less cluttered, and dare I say it, better. Maybe that’s the millennial in me who yearns for everything from my childhood to be brought back and forced on younger generations. That page of neatly arranged links and descriptions just looks more appealing to me than the modern-day alternative filled with images, ads, and an AI overview I didn’t ask for.

While naturally all of the search results are about Ocarina of Time, they don’t appear to be curated for its time capsule page. The news about someone sharing footage early is on there, which is definitely not something Google and Nintendo would have wanted to include if the 1998 version of the page included predetermined search results.

Unfortunately, you don’t seem to be able to keep Google’s 1998 de-makeover indefinitely. As soon as you search for something else and click on one of those chunky grey buttons, you’re returned to 2026 in the blink of an eye. You can also revert the page back to the way it’s supposed to be by clicking the Master Sword again, although if anyone from Google is reading this, I'd love a way for my Google to look like it never changed after 1998, and I bet I'm not the only one.

#4249. Digital Foundry Delivers Its Tech Verdict On Call Of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 On Switch 2

Just in case the news passed you by, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 launched on Switch 2 this month — the first in the series to do so since the Wii U days. Naturally, a lot of the attention has been on the game's performance and whether the Switch 2 would be able to keep up with its competitors. Here to answer exactly that are the tech experts over at Digital Foundry, who have just shared their thoughts on the hybrid version's nitty-gritty details.

We'll start with the all-important frame rates. DF states that MW4 runs at 30fps in its campaign mode, 60fps in competitive multiplayer, and 40fps (if you have a 120Hz display hooked up) in the DMZ extraction mode. While this is a little lower than other platforms — particularly in the campaign respect — it does mean that we Switch 2 players can still get the full-fat CoD experience.

It's all relatively stable, too. In the campaign, you'll see hitching in pre-rendered cutscenes (also found on other platforms), though actual gameplay isn't affected, and things run at a smooth 30. The same can be said for the DMZ mode at 40fps — though there is obviously a little input latency for both by opting for a locked, lower rate.

Things occasionally drop into the 50s or even high-40s in online multiplayer, with input latency adding "an extra challenge in getting the best kill-to-death ratio".

There are two anti-aliasing options in the Switch 2 version, running at a dynamic 900p in DLSS mode (dropping to 450p in "the worst cases") and at a higher 1080p target when using the SMAA T2X mode. In handheld, it runs at a dynamic 720p, dropping to 360p in more intense missions.

There are some cutbacks, of course. Asset resolution is noticeably lower than on other platforms when crouching, and some reflections lose a lot of detail. There are lower-quality shadows (there aren't any on the player character in the campaign mode), and you will notice more pop-in detail jumps on Switch 2.

That said, DF considers it a "job well done", all in all, keeping all of the important elements in place — which proves key for keeping things balanced in cross-platform online play.

We had a great time with Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2, calling it "an excellent demonstration of why this crusty series still matters to so many" in our 9/10 review.

#4248. The Blood Of Dawnwalker Update 1.1 Adds Quality Of Life Improvements, Boosts Performance, and Adds Pettable Animals

We've been enjoying The Blood of Dawnwalker, one of the year's biggest games, but its release was a little rough around the edges. It took a lot of feedback from fans for developer Rebel Wolves to prioritize higher framerates at launch for consoles, but even then, the game certainly struggled at times on my PlayStation 5. Today, the game's first major update drops, and it aims to smooth some of those performance issues and introduce a few quality-of-life features.

The trailer above highlights combat-specific improvements, like improved targeting and animations, and a less restrictive camera. Rebel Wolves is also lowering the health of wolves and boars, who previously remained tanky even into the later hours of the game, and it should be easier to disengage from combat, should you choose to do so. For casual players, there's a new difficulty mode; what was previously "Story" mode has been renamed "Forgiving," while the new version of "Story" mode adds additional combat assists.

Rebel Wolves has also added some new features outside of combat. A new Daught of Mind Rebirth potion allows you to respec your skill tree, re-allocating time and skill points spent to switch up your build. You can also increase the size of subtitles (an option I'm always grateful for) and pet dogs and cats. Finally, the Shadowstep and Planeshift systems should be more responsive now – here's hoping I have an easier time teleporting onto rooftops instead of the wall right below them.

Those are the major, most visible highlights, but players can view the full patch notes here to see the hundreds of other minor improvements that aim to squash bugs, reduce crashes, and improve stability.

For more on The Blood of Dawnwalker, you can check out our review, in which our reviewer admires the swings the developers took, even though they don't always pay off. You can also check out our coverage hub for our issue devoted to The Blood of Dawnwalker, including interviews with its ex-Witcher development team.

#4247. Battlefield 6's next season will speed up battle pass progression, and make it so Redsec players who don't own the game can actually make progress

Season 2 of Battlefield 6 looks to bring a host of broad, positive changes to XP, progression, audio and more.

Ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch. The game’s second season was delayed in mid-January, and the developer even brought back Battlefield Labs to test out some of the new content and features coming with the new season.

Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a new blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing issues with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.

We know that Season 2 is introducing a big new map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing. The map will indeed arrive in the first part of the season, and it’s going to do so alongside a new LTM that “introduces a new element of tactics.” A second, “high-intensity map” will debut later into the season, alongside another LTM where players battle through an underground base, in darkness.

The real meat of the blog post, however, covers the broader gameplay changes everyone will see once the new season kicks off. There’s a massive focus on player progression, especially when it concerns free-to-play Redsec players.

Challenges are being streamlined yet again, with more broad parameters that don’t require specific modes. Some, like dailies, will also allow for assists to count towards their criteria. Less restrictive challenges are welcome, but even more so is the faster battle pass progression.

BF Studios is changing the rate at which battle pass Tokens are earned from career XP, and making it so they’re earnable by playing the game normally, and by completing weekly challenges. These changes should also help Redsec players, who will also benefit from faster career and weapon XP earn rates - across both battle royale, and Gauntlet. In general, the career experience should feel more rewarding, especially for earlier ranks.

Weapon balance and recoil are two areas that will continue to evolve in Battlefield 6, it seems, and Season 2 is specifically tackling recoil patterns to make them more consistent when you compensate for them.

Movement is being adjusted with the Season 2 patch, too, though thankfully it’s limited to general feel that touches areas like vaulting, ladder transitions, and acceleration curves. You should also see better continuity and consistency between animations and feel.

Audio is getting a pass with the upcoming patch, especially when it comes to footstep and interaction audio. This also extends to something the developer has been working on improving for a while, and it has to do with how the game decides which audio tracks to prioritise in busy situations.

Tomorrow, the full Battlefield 6 Season 2 trailer will be released, while a more detailed roadmap is expected by the end of this week.

#4246. Dispatch's Anniversary Update Brings Commentary Track, Storyboard Mode, And Mobile Port

Dispatch, a superhero-themed workplace comedy from last year, celebrates its one-year anniversary today. While it was released episodically, the first batch dropped on October 22. It was received well, with strong performances from a star-studded cast (including Breaking Bad star Aaron Paul) and filled a niche left vacant by Telltale Games' absence from the gaming world in recent years. Today, developer AdHoc announced a batch of anniversary content, and some of it drops today.

First, there's a new way to play Dispatch: storyboard mode. This option lets you play through the whole experience using the original animatics – rough placeholder sketches that the artists used to sync images up to the voice-over. It's a fun behind-the-scenes look at the game's development that we don't get very often. In that same vein, the cast and crew recorded DVD-style commentary tracks to play over the game, making jokes and sharing insight into the development process. A press release says there are over 16 hours of commentary from the game's development team (like art director Derek Stratton and creative directors Dennis Lenart and Nick Herman) as well as some of the cast, including Aaron Paul, Laura Bailey, and Erin Yvette.

Storyboard and Commentary modes are included in the game's deluxe edition, which you can upgrade to for $10.99. Both modes are available today.

If you haven't played the game yet, AdHoc has announced a new way to do so; Dispatch is coming to mobile platforms on December 9. It's been rebuilt to support touch controls and vertical play, and it will be available on iOS and Android. You can even play the first half of the game for free – the first four episodes are included, but you'll need to pay $19.99 to play the rest.

Finally, AdHoc announced new merch, including a book created alongside publisher Lost in Cult called Dispatch: Design Works, which is both an art book and a "making-of" book. There's also a live game soundtrack concert in Los Angeles featuring Thot Squad, Bershy, Primer, Caroline Kingsbury, Fartbarf, and Dispatch composer Andrew Arcadi with the SDN Company Band. It will be held at Avalon Hollywood on December 3, but it won't be livestreamed, so you'll need to grab a ticket to see the event. The press release states that people who signed up for updates from adhocstudio.com will be the first in line to purchase tickets.

#4245. Diablo 4’s next class is the Warlock, but you can sort of play it today in Diablo 2: Resurrected’s new DLC

Blizzard has officially unveiled the Warlock, the second class coming to Diablo 4 with Lord of Hatred.

Diablo 4’s segment in the big Diablo 30th Anniversary Spotlight was among the biggest, even if the reason most of us tuned in was somewhat spoiled earlier in the same livestream. Blizzard unveiled the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The first class, being the Paladin, is already available to play for anyone who pre-ordered the expansion, but the Warlock won’t be accessible until the expansion arrives in late April.

The Warlocks are positioned as the opposite of the Paladins, in that they don’t mind utilising forbidden knowledge, drawing on the powers of Hell itself to fight its own overlords. The Warlock is the edgy, antihero counterpart to the Paladin’s purity and devotion to the Light.

The livestream did not show off any Warlock gameplay, but Blizzard is planning a dedicated livestream to show off the new class’ gameplay, and dig deeper into its lore and abilities. That show is scheduled for March 5.

What we did get to see was our first look at Skovos, the expansion’s new region. This Mediterranean-inspired location is where the new story arc will unfold, but it’s also being positioned as the endgame destination for Diablo 4 once the credits roll.

Lord of Hatred, of course, as previously revealed, introduces two new endgame modes in War Plans, and Echoing Hatred.

War Plans lets you create a custom playlist of up to five endgame activities to target specific rewards and create your own experience. There’s a new activity tree that works with all endgame activities, and creating War Plans is how you earn progression there.

Echoing Hatred, on the other hand, is a rare event that pits you against legions of Mephisto’s minions. It’s triggered through a rare lootable item that unlocks access. It’s essentially horde mode; where you’ll face unending waves of enemies, though not without a couple of twists.

We also got a bit more colour on the expanded class skill trees, which all players will benefit from when the expansion arrives. The Talisman system, which unlocks set bonuses, was also shown off. And, of course, the return of the iconic Horadric Cube, which gives you control over Affixes.

The Anniversary Spotlight should’ve had a Year of the Warlock subtitle, because the class is also making its way to both Diablo Immortal, as well as Diablo 2: Resurrected. The showcase revealed the Reign of the Warlock DLC, which adds the aforementioned Warlock to D2R - its first new class in 25 years.

Reign of the Warlock, which is available now in D2R, also makes a few updates to the game, such as new quality of life features, the Colossal Ancients endgame encounter, updated Terror Zones and more. You also get some cosmetics in Diablo 4 if you purchase this expansion.

#4242. 10 Best JRPGs for Players New to the Genre

Melissa Sarnowski is a Gaming Writer at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2022. She specializes in lists, reviews, and features, with additional experience writing guides for Hardcore Gamer.

JRPGs can be intimidating if you're first looking to get into the genre. There are so many series, and for some of them, it's difficult to know where you should start and which order to play in. Then, you have franchises like Final Fantasy with standalone games numbered in a way that makes it seem like you have to go in order if you aren't familiar with the series.

Here are the most addictive JRPGs that you can play on the PlayStation 5 right now.

Regardless of the genre, figuring out a new subset of games you might not have explored previously can be overwhelming at first. That's especially true when you consider that opinions about games tend to be quite strong, making it seem like a game is worse than it actually is.

If you like Disney, then this is definitely where you should start your exploration of JRPGs. Plus, there's a fourth game in the works, so this is the perfect time to try the series and get familiar with it before the next one comes out.

Kingdom Hearts is a blend between Disney and Final Fantasy. You find characters from both franchises alongside new characters, giving you some familiarity from the start. Plus, you don't need to know anything about Final Fantasy going into the game, and you'll still understand what's going on. The overarching story does become more convoluted as the series goes on, though.

Hear me out on this one. Final Fantasy 14 is technically an MMO, and I could understand an argument that it doesn't count as a JRPG. However, it includes a lot of story elements and recurring characters and bosses that you find in the overall franchise.

Thanks to this critically acclaimed MMORPG having a free trial through Shadowbringers without a limit on playtime, you can experience a bit of what Final Fantasy can be like without spending money, then decide if you want to dive into the JRPGs of the franchise. There's so much content to dive into if you like what you find.

Like Kingdom Hearts, Pokémon Sword and Shield are a great starting point for JRPGs if you're already familiar with the Pokémon franchise through the show, toys, other games, or anything else related to it. That familiarity makes it less intimidating to get started.

Sword and Shield are some of the more beginner-friendly games that give you an idea of how the more classic options in the series feel, but with a modern polish that eliminates parts that might otherwise be frustrating. They aren't perfect, but they're solid choices for a beginner. It's a solid take on JRPG combat to teach you about exploiting weaknesses, avoiding your own, and so on.

Honestly, you could pick any game from the Dragon Quest series. I just chose Dragon Quest 11 because it's among the easier ones to access in the series. It's also considered a masterpiece JRPG, as an added bonus. For a good first impression of the genre, it's difficult to find better.

DQ11 in particular has turn-based combat with a bit of a faster pace, which might be preferable if you're used to more hack-and-slash or action-oriented styles of combat. Combined with the usual Dragon Quest charm and a beautiful world, you have a game that makes it easy to fall in love with JRPGs. The story's engaging too.

I would put Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave here, because it also has a lot of built-in time for you to explore the world and has some simulator elements included, like Three Houses. Fortune's Weave is only on the Nintendo Switch 2, however, making Three Houses the somewhat more accessible option.

Fire Emblem as a series includes a lot of the most classic JRPG elements, and people tend to love the characters and their storylines. You have turn-based combat and have to strategize to win. As a bonus, if you like one Fire Emblem, you'll probably like others, making it a good first step into the genre. There's a huge amount of content here, too.

There's something so quaint about the Octopath Traveler games that I can't quite explain. It uses Square Enix’s HD-2D style that brings 3D environments to the classic 16-bit pixel world. The result is a game that feels both modern and nostalgic.

It's hard to go wrong with Octopath Traveler. You have eight characters that each have a unique storyline and abilities. Those abilities are important both in and out of combat, as you can use different characters for tasks in towns, like stealing items or starting duels. You have to be strategic, but you also get to be creative, and that's valuable. You want to have fun and not just get stuck grinding.

While any game from the Persona series is a good starting point, Persona 5 usually gets the spotlight. However, Persona 3 Reload offers a modernized version of the original game, so you could honestly pick either one and get a feeling for JRPGs in a more familiar school setting and a coming-of-age story.

Just because they’re RPGs inspired by Japanese culture doesn’t mean they automatically have anime aesthetics.

The feature that makes Persona so beginner-friendly is its social sim mechanics. It isn't just about improving your strength in this series; you also want to improve your relationships with those around you, perhaps find love, and fulfill your obligations as a student at school. You can engage with as much as you wish.

Often considered one of the greatest JRPGs of all time, it doesn't get more classic than Chrono Trigger. If you want to dive right into the genre and experience what the games in it were like in the 1990s and early 2000s, then this is the game you want.

You have the turn-based combat, multiple party members who each have their own strengths, the blend of sci-fi and fantasy that JRPGs love using, and even time travel. It hits all the classic JRPG features, without the bloat that tends to creep into games of this sort. A legendary starting point.

Final Fantasy 7 is a fan favorite of the series, and it's an interesting option in that you can play the original and experience the classic JRPG style, or you can play the remake trilogy to experience a more modern JRPG. They're both great options.

Because players like to be spoiled by great graphics and massive open worlds, I’d almost suggest playing the available games of the remake trilogy first, which are going to be more familiar if you're used to modern games and not used to JRPGs. If you enjoy it, you can always explore the rest of the games connected to FF7, and you'll be ready when FF7 Revelations is released to complete the trilogy.

Despite being remade for the Nintendo Switch, I feel like Super Mario RPG is often forgotten when you talk about JRPGs, because this usually isn't the genre that Mario shows up in. You'll look at platformers and adventure genres to find Mario games first, not JRPGs.

However, Super Mario RPG is a great pick partially for that reason. The characters and world are familiar from the start because Mario as a franchise is so well-known. Now, you just have that content arranged into a game with JRPG features like a focus on narrative and turn-based combat.

Gaming has so much to offer that players can almost always find a genre that resonates with them, but sometimes you want to look beyond your usual options and try something new. If JRPGs are what you're looking at trying, it's tough to know where to start. However, there are so many masterpieces that it's worth finding the right game to introduce you to the genre.

JRPGs are an acquired taste for some, but these games are tasty no matter what.

#4241. Tenebris Somnia Review – A Hair-Raising And Entertaining Throwback

Tenebris Somnia channels the old-school appeal of classic point-and-click adventures, survival horror, and full-motion-video (FMV) experiences, then smartly modernizes them to create a creepy, entertaining experience. Surviving the twisted threats of a demonic dream world is a tightly packed adventure that rewards you with what’s essentially an impressive indie horror film peppered throughout. It’s a nightmare you may not want to wake up from.

The blend of live-action and in-game storytelling works well in Tenebris Somina’s adventure, which begins when protagonist Julia visits the apartment of her filmmaker ex-boyfriend, Ivan, after suffering recurring nightmares of him being massacred by monsters. What begins as a well-meaning check-in on his status spirals down an unsettling rabbit hole when Julia’s worst fears are realized and then some. The dialogue-free tale presents a scary but fascinating exploration of obsession, both in art and in romance, that constantly delivers surprising, and at times upsetting, revelations during its eight-hour runtime. While Tenebris Somnia sometimes leans a little too far into “tell, don’t show” territory when explaining the cool lore of its supernatural threats, I never felt lost or confused about the wild things that regularly unfold on screen.

FMV experiences are nothing new, but Tenebris Somnia’s live-action scenes are a highlight. They’re well shot, sport impressively gruesome practical effects, and even present visual clues that make them important to gameplay. These scenes are additive, never taking too much time away from the in-game action, and they feel well placed to elicit the strongest emotional response. I also appreciate how the live scenes fit thematically, as much of Tenebris Somnia’s tale centers on a horror film shot by Ivan and Julia that significantly impacted their former relationship; at times, it’s like watching a movie about the movie. While I enjoy smaller moments, like opening a door to trigger a live-action jump scare, the filmmaking succeeds in selling Julia's emotions and the cast's reactions. Seeing real fear, concern, and determination in Julia’s eyes as she navigates a dreamworld made up of Ivan’s memories helped endear me to what would otherwise be a featureless pixel sprite.

Gameplay may look unimpressive due to its old-school adventure game presentation, but Tenebris Somnia’s spin on familiar survival-horror mechanics hits the right notes. Taking place entirely within a dreamlike version of a four-story apartment building, you’ll traverse floors collecting and combining objects and deciphering clues to solve well-crafted puzzles. I’m impressed by how well the game’s puzzles make the most of its limited graphical presentation, including clever scenarios involving mirror/screen reflections I won’t spoil, and how consistently creative they are. One devious exercise even utilizes the game’s limited save points as an unexpected resource in a way that changes how you approach your adventure going forward. No matter how strange puzzles become, they are never opaque, requiring just enough out-of-the-box thinking to make me feel smart when I connect the dots.

Battling grotesque monsters (which, naturally, look even creepier in live-action) also feels good, with melee and gunplay sporting deliberate animations reminiscent of classic adventure games without feeling mechanically clunky. Taking on multiple enemies by swinging a pipe or blowing them away with a shotgun feels better than it looks, and the most intense encounters end just as they approach the line of becoming overwhelming.

Boss battles, perhaps most unexpectedly for a largely puzzle-focused adventure, are fun and distinct from each other, be it wave-based bouts against small gremlin-like foes, protecting a fragile effigy of yourself from a parade of demented house servants, or battling literal mirror images of a tentacled flesh monster the Resident Evil series would be proud to claim. Managing limited ammo and health strikes a good balance of feeling tense but not oppressive. Playing conservatively is rewarding, as few non-boss threats need to be engaged if you can evade them well enough. But when I did find myself down to my last bullet or on the verge of death, Tenebris Somnia lets you feel the pinch just long enough before dropping a box of bullets or a health vial at the right moment.

Tenebris Somnia mines the enjoyable nostalgia of playing the horror games of yesteryear without feeling dated in the worst way. Weaving a solid indie horror film adds to the experience rather than feeling like a gimmick. The result is a captivating, well-executed survival-horror romp that maintains a hair-raising atmosphere with a fraction of the pixels of other genre giants.

#4240. A Mass Effect 5 Trailer Featuring Liara Appears To Have Leaked Following BioWare's Closure

In case you missed the tragic news yesterday, EA laid off 400 employees this week, including all of BioWare. The studio behind Mass Effect, Dragon Age, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and more, has been shut down, and its last remaining project was canceled. The game in question was a fifth entry in the Mass Effect universe, and BioWare shared very little about it – not even an official name. Following the studio's closure, however, a trailer for the sci-fi sequel started circulating around the internet.

While no official BioWare representatives have confirmed that the footage is real, Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier claims that it is. Schreier has a history of credible reporting in the field, and was the first to break the news about the layoffs. IGN has also stated that it confirmed the trailer's legitimacy.

If you want to see for yourself, you can watch the trailer on Reddit.

"The following is in-engine footage form our small team," text at the start of the video reads. "It uses our pre-production assets." The footage shows no gameplay, but includes a good-looking CG cutscene of a new protagonist speaking with an asari woman in a crowded bar. As he tells her about his life, we see glimpses of him as a soldier, then as some kind of spy, traveling to several planets to track down conflicts and "stopping them before they start." After the asari woman reveals that she's been "starting the fires" he's trying to prevent, another woman behind her lowers a hood. This new woman reveals herself as Liara T'Soni, one of Mass Effect's most iconic characters.

Then, Liara and the protagonist team up to take out the woman at the bar and her henchmen, using guns and telekinetic abilities. The trailer fades to black, then fades back in to reveal the game's would-be title: Mass Effect Universe. It's a great-looking trailer – it's a shame the game will never see the light of day.

If you want to join us in grieving BioWare, we republished an oral history of the studio that was originally written by former editor Matt Bertz in 2016. You can also read our cover stories on BioWare's most recent releases: Dragon Age: The Veilguard, Mass Effect: Legendary Edition, Anthem, and Mass Effect Andromeda.

#4236. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Review - Silver Bullet

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 arrives at a crossroads for the series, thanks in large part to the inconsistent quality of recent entries. With a shaky predecessor, Infinity Ward had a lot to repair and conclude, especially with 4 set to bookend the rebooted Modern Warfare series. Fortunately, backed up by a fun campaign, thrilling multiplayer, and loads of new modes and content, Modern Warfare 4 makes up for the past and then some.

Modern Warfare 4 continues after the events of 2023’s Modern Warfare 3, with Captain Price hellbent on stopping Makarov and his higher-ups. The story features shifting perspectives, from a new group of ragtag Korean soldiers to familiar characters like Gaz. The character dynamics harken back to the original trilogy, especially in the boots-on-the-ground missions with the South Korean unit, led by Park (played by Beef actor Young Mazino).

For a series that, at least recently, has been more spectacle than story, giving the stakes the time they deserve is nice. While it moves away from the stealthy and modernized elements, it makes sense for the matters at hand. The majority of Modern Warfare 4’s attempts at wrapping up the overarching plot of the rebooted series works, but it rushes through some character arcs and story beats in uneven fashion. Furthermore, much of the game’s cast, especially Mads Mikkelson’s Archer and Prisca Kim’s Ri Ju-Young, are underutilized, which is a shame since they both deliver great performances.

Despite the shortcomings of the campaign, Call of Duty's bread and butter, multiplayer, still delivers. While it doesn’t have the fluidity of Black Ops’ newer entries, the customization and design of weapons and maps make it worth digging into. From small, intimate shooting galleries with Mumbai and Nautical to wide free-for-alls like Coal and Reactor U92, the range helps maintain excitement, even if it gets repetitive over time.

The variety of multiplayer modes keeps things fresh on the battlefield. Returning modes like standard Team Deathmatch and Kill Confirmed continue that enjoyable competitive flair that made them the stars that they are. However, new modes like Combat Outpost and Hijack fit right into the already great lineup. In particular, Combat Outpost upscales your typical 6v6 player count to 24v24, leading to more action and teamwork. Hanging onto a team’s tank, shooting enemies from afar, and taking back outposts is exhilarating, even if it can all go bad moments later by a well-placed RPG shot.

Even after hours of gameplay, the variety of options to craft your perfect gun is impressive. Figuring out the best scope, ammo, stock, and muzzle, as well as the advantages and disadvantages of them, is a fun way of customizing your playstyle. Gunny, a mechanic that helps optimize your gun for certain styles, can help with decision paralysis, but I rarely used it. Not many FPSs go that far and Modern Warfare 4’s commitment to the feature makes it stand out.

The newest mode, DMZ, impresses out of the gate. After a few flat attempts in the past, this is the definitive Call of Duty extraction shooter, whether you play solo, or in duos or trios. Immediately, you’re thrust into the wide open world of Hajin and left to fend for yourselves with what you have and what you can gather and extract. Fans of Arc Raiders and Marathon should feel right at home as the gameplay borrows from the typical extraction shooter experience. Intense, action-packed moments keep you coming back after every win or loss. And the excellent gunplay and level design elevate it into something worthwhile, no matter how you play.

Despite not encountering many live players during my time in Hajin in DMZ, it still proves challenging, even for seasoned pros. The world is not your friend, and taking risks can come at a high cost. A good team, as well as a thoughtful loadout and traits, are required to survive. The unpredictability of it all keeps you on your toes, making for an exciting addition to the already strong multiplayer suite.

Regardless of the mode, Modern Warfare 4 is one of the best-looking Call of Duty titles to date. New York and Paris are lifelike, and it truly embodies the realistic, modern aesthetic the series has always aimed to achieve. However, I encountered a few technical hiccups, especially in the campaign. Slow framerate plagues some high-octane scenes and texture loading is frequent across the board. These distractions are far from game-breaking, but enough to be noticeable.

While the plot execution is a bit shaky, engaging multiplayer options, including DMZ, aptly demonstrate that Infinity Ward can still deliver compelling military-FPS experiences. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is a strong return to form that serves as a solid sendoff for the rebooted subseries.

#4235. 8 Switch Metroidvanias That Respect Your Time

Shayna Josi is a Contributor at DualShockers who covers RPGs, cozy games, life sims, action games, gamer culture, and PC gaming. She has been writing professionally since 2020 and covering games since 2023, with a focus on features, commentary, storytelling, character writing, and game design.

People are busy and don’t have time to sink hundredss of hours into a game. I love a sprawling game, but every single one boasting a hundred-hour-long campaign is just not feasible. It’s even worse when the game is artificially bloated with bad check points and constant backtracking.

Stardew Valley keeps rewarding players who pay attention. After hundreds of hours, there might still be details hiding in plain sight.

There are a lot of Metroidvanias that take a long time to complete, but not all of them are massive time sinks. There are some Metroidvanias that have either streamlined their mechanics for easier gameplay, or they’re short and sweet. If you're looking for a Switch Metroidvania that respects your time, these ones are well worth considering.

Not every Metroidvania needs to be brutally difficult to be rewarding, and a lot of the time small games punch above their weight class. Islets is one such game —it's a charming adventure with very forgiving combat and random time limited upgrades that affect exploration and your combat capabilities. While you still need to learn attack patterns for boss fights, it’s significantly less difficult than most other Metroidvanias.

Islets also has great level design, which uses an interconnected structure that gives you plenty of reasons to revisit locations you’ve already visited. Doing so isn’t unnecessarily complicated, and having a reason to backtrack makes it feel worthwhile rather than a slog.

Sometimes, the best way to respect the player's time is to deliver a fantastic experience and know when to end it. Gato Roboto is a short Metroidvania that ends on a high note, before it overstays its welcome.

Gato Roboto’s monochromatic presentation gives it a distinctive retro aesthetic, and being able to play as a cat is charming and fun. The environments are relatively compact, which makes sense for a small creature like a cat, but that also makes for straightforward navigation. You'll still discover new abilities and encounter challenging bosses, but the adventure rarely feels like it's padding its runtime with unnecessary bloat.

Record of Lodoss War: Deedlit in Wonder Labyrinth is a relatively short Metroidvania that makes its inspiration from Castlevania games more obvious even than other Metroidvania games. Its environments and progression system make it a good choice if you want a focused adventure.

There are a lot of video games out there that instill a sense of discovery in its players, but not every single one can be called a Metroidvania.

Record of Lodoss War: Deedlit in Wonder Labyrinth is short and sweet: it can be completed in approximately five to six hours, depending on how much time you spend exploring. Its story is straightforward, which means it's perfect if you want to turn your brain off and focus on combat. Because it's so short, it's perfect for a weekend or a night in.

Touhou Luna Nights takes a particularly interesting approach to Metroidvania combat because it introduces time manipulation as one of its central mechanics. As you progress through the levels, you'll encounter increasingly challenging enemies and bosses that require you to understand how your time-manipulation abilities work.

The mechanic is particularly effective because it influences almost every aspect of the experience, a sign of good game design and makes sure that every mechanic does something productive. Touhou Luna Nights is also relatively short, taking approximately five hours to complete. The intentional design means you can enjoy it without having to spend dozens of hours working through repetitive encounters.

If you're looking for a Metroidvania that prioritizes combat and movement, Blade Chimera is worth checking out. Blade Chimera combines the traditional Metroidvania level design with a unique weapon mechanic that changes up combat and makes it more interesting.

Because of its focus on the weapon mechanic, there's also considerable emphasis on responsive combat and movement. Its progression system gives you opportunities to improve your character's capabilities without making repetitive grinding the central focus of the experience. This is the perfect game if you like Metroidvania combat without the frustration you get in Soulslikes. The warp skill makes travel instantaneous, and removes a lot of needless repetition.

Astalon: Tears of the Earth is one of the more traditional Metroidvanias on this list. It shows that good level design can make longer games feel short, and it does that by centering its exploration around a tower. Because you can freely switch between three characters with different abilities, there's some strategy required to excel in this game.

Although it may not seem like it, these adventures are essential to play if you're a fan of the genre.

Astalon is considerably more challenging and demanding than many other Metroidvanias, but its carefully constructed environments make the additional time feel purposeful. It's a great choice if you enjoy that classic Metroidvania design and want something that offers a little more depth.

Ori and the Blind Forest is one of those games that changes you. It's a whimsical, beautiful, and emotional experience, and yet it also understands the importance of maintaining momentum, something that's crucial for good game design. Because of this, its exploration feels like an important part of the journey, rather than something you have to endure between major encounters.

Ori avoids tedious backtracking with a Soul Link checkpoint system, which lets you place your own checkpoints. This gives you considerably more control over your progress and allows you to prepare for particularly challenging sections. It's just one mechanic that forms the greater whole of a good game.

Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown is arguably one of the best examples of a modern Metroidvania that respects the player's time. While its interconnected world is packed with things to do, it also includes several quality-of-life mechanics that make exploration considerably less frustrating.

One of these mechanics is the Memory Shard system, which allows you to simply refer back to your screenshots when you've acquired the necessary abilities. Guided Mode is also a big help, as it shows you where to go next without forcing you to follow a predetermined route. These mechanics guide you rather than hold your hand, but they're a lifesaver that stops you from getting stuck in one place for hours and reaching for a guide.

#4234. You're not crazy, trying to heal in Nioh 3 sometimes doesn't work - and Team Ninja is fixing it

One of the more insidiously aggravating bugs in Nioh 3 makes it so the game ignores you when you try to use elixirs, but hopefully not for long.

Nioh 3 has received a hot new update that brings plenty of bug fixes to very specific issues, but it also implements fixes for a few of the most common - and incredibly annoying - bugs. Patch 1.03.01 arrived earlier on all platforms, and it comes with a chunky set of notes.

This latest update, predictably, doesn’t add any gameplay features, but some of the included fixes will absolutely delight - or vindicate - so many of the game’s millions of players.

There’s plenty to go through in the patch notes published today for update 1.03.01, but the most impactful is a fix for an issue that “sometimes made it impossible to use elixirs during battle.” This is only a partial fix, but if you ran into the problem of smashing that shortcut button and not seeing your character play the healing animation, you’ll be glad to see it.

This is a problem myself and others have faced, especially in boss fights. You can even see the shortcut register your button press and proceed to ignore you. Another partial fix has been made to an issue that caused the game to crash. Team Ninja didn’t share specifics on that, and though Nioh 3 has been fairly stable for me in 70+ hours, it has definitely crashed a few times.

If you’ve been playing since launch, you likely have - or know someone who has - run into issues with save file corruption and other weird bugs around certain trackable items within save files.

Team Ninja already rolled out a couple of fixes there, and this latest one specifically targets losing valuables during Myths. If your save file has been affected, the game will now check and recover what was lost. Even more interesting is that the game will now automatically create a backup copy of your save data any time you load a save.

If you’ve made it into the Eternal Rift, you’ll be happy to know that today’s update takes care of a few progression blockers, and fixes an issue that allowed some players to obtain certain items before they were supposed to, locking themselves out.

One of the more amusing fixes concerns Mujina, who had a tendency to respawn if you prayed at a Shrine after opening a chest it was hiding in, which made it appear far more often than a mimic should.

Finally, there’s a set of fixes that address bugs (and exploits) when using specific Martial Art with certain weapons. There are a few fixes to AI, Myths, and one problem with the Minamoto no Yoritomo boss fight that made it impossible to interrupt him, even after he runs out of Ki.

Hit the link at the top for the full change log, and check out our Nioh 3 gameplay tips if you haven’t already. You should also change these settings ASAP, as they’re going to make your life much easier and save you a lot of time.

#4233. Amazon’s Mass Effect TV Series Is Reportedly Still In Production Despite BioWare Closure

EA shut down legendary RPG developer BioWare this week, canceling its in-development fifth Mass Effect game as a result. Despite the closure, Amazon Prime’s upcoming Mass Effect streaming series will proceed as planned, according to a report by IGN.

Amazon MGM Studios began developing a Mass Effect series in 2024. At the time, Mass Effect series executive producer Mike Gamble confirmed the show isn't a retelling of the video games, saying, “The show will explore a brand-new story within the universe's timeline, and will be set after the original trilogy. It won't be a retread of Commander Shepard's story – because after all... that's YOUR story, isn’t it?”

With BioWare’s closure, one would think the series would go up in smoke, but sources within Prime Video speaking to IGN confirmed that it remains in development. Furthermore, all of the creatives involved remain so. This includes showrunners Doug Jung (The Cloverfield Paradox, Star Trek Beyond) and Daniel Casey (F9: The Fast Saga, Wardriver), former Marvel Studios head Avi Arad, and Jessica Jones executive producer Karim Zreik. Mike Gamble was also involved, and this report suggests he still is, but it remains to be seen how his position on the project has changed with BioWare’s demise, given he served as a guiding voice from the studio. The Mass Effect series has no release window.

The Mass Effect series joins other video game adaptations Amazon has in the works, which include a third season of Fallout (with Aaron Paul joining the cast), a live-action God of War series starring Dave Bautista, a live-action Tomb Raider series starring Sophie Turner, as well as series based on Life is Strange and Wolfenstein.

For more on Mass Effect, check out our review of the Legendary Edition and our recently republished Oral History of BioWare from 2016.

The team is also working on "more post-release features"

Mina The Hollower has been digitally available for Switch 1 & 2 since May, and if you're wondering about the status of the physical edition, you're not alone.

During a chat with the Switch community on Reddit this week, developer Yacht Club Games has reassured fans it's "still planned". Company founder Sean Velasco says the team is working on finding the right publishing and distribution partner:

"Yes! It’s still planned. We’re working on finding the right publishing and distribution partner to make it happen. No release date to share yet, but it’s absolutely still in progress!

As for the physical version's release window, it sounds like fans can expect it by next year. Yacht Club has already released some Mina the Hollower merch via Fangamer and a soundtrack vinyl on iam8bit, and an art book is also on the way.

During the same chat, Yacht Club mentioned how it's currently working on "more post-release features" and "some quality of life and accessibility content updates to polish the full experience", while reiterating there are no plans for DLC right now:

"Nothing to announce on DLC right now, but we’re working on more post-release features! Expanded randomizer options, enemy and boss randomization, more modifiers, speedrunner features... lots of ways to do even more in Mina."

So, when the physical version of Mina the Holllower does eventually arrive, it will hopefully be the definitive version of the game.

#4231. How To Get Ocarina Of Time Remake's N64 Slip Cover Pre-Order Bonus In The UK

The Ocarina of Time remake is still a few days away, which means it’s not too late to pre-order your copy and secure whichever bonus comes with doing that in your part of the world. Unfortunately, the best bonuses of all, those N64 slip covers, are tied to retailers in France and Canada. However, Nintendo has just announced a way to get your hands on one in the UK.

It is going to require a little more than just buying your copy of the Ocarina remake from a specific retailer, though, and potentially even some travel depending on where you live. Argos, specifically the store on Tottenham Court Road in London, will be holding a midnight launch of the new Switch 2 exclusive. That’s where you’ll need to go if you want one of those slip covers.

The midnight launch, which will take place at midnight UK time on November 5, Ocarina launch day, is open to anyone and everyone. Buy your copy of the Ocarina remake at the launch event, and it will come with a free N64 slip cover for the game and an Ocarina keychain. It’s the black and gold cover, as that’s the version the original game had in the UK and Europe.

The only way to get the red and gold slip cover pre-order bonus is by buying the remake through EB Games in Canada.

There is neither a ticket to buy nor even a box to check to indicate if you’re attending, which means no way of knowing how many people are going to be queuing outside of that Argos until Wednesday night. That, in turn, means there’s no guarantee you’ll get one of those covers if you show up. While you’d hope Argos and Nintendo have printed more of the covers than they could ever need, there’s a very real chance so many people show up that they run out of them.

If you’re in the UK but you can’t make it to London for Argos’s midnight opening, and you can’t get the sought-after slipcover, there is still a regular pre-order bonus up for grabs. Buy the game before release day, and it will come with some Spirit Stone replicas.

There are other pre-order bonuses available elsewhere around the world. Too many to list here, although we have a dedicated article covering all of them and where you need to live to get them. The ones Zelda fans want most, though, do still seem to be those N64 covers.

#4230. Genshin Impact Luna 5 takes the squad back to Mondstadt, finally makes Varka playable

Genshin Impact's next update will have you reminiscing about the good ol' days of... 2020.

The latest big content update has been revealed for HoYoverse's breakout game, Genshin Impact. Version Luna 5, which has the unusually long and needlessly layered title — Song of the Welkin Moon: Variation - Homeward, He Who Caught the Wind — is set to arrive February 25.

This one is a bit of a nostalgia play, taking everyone back to Mondstadt, the place where you may remember taking your first steps. And, as with any good return to the ol’ hunting grounds, come familiar characters, too.

The big new arrival is Varka, who joins as a playable character for the first time. Varka, Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius, is a character whose debut has been long-awaited. He is a 5-Star Anemo Claymore wielder with a dual-wield combat style, capable of dealing two different types of Elemental damage. His addition means that there's now finally a burly 5-Star male character of each elemental type... do with that information what you will.

Varka's dual-wielding combat style allows him to deal two different types of Elemental damage at the same time. The way it works is that his Elemental Skill boosts the damage of his regular attacks, but it also converts the damage type of his right-hand claymore to match his teammates’ elements (Pyro, Hydro, Electro, or Cryo). The left-hand claymore always deals Anemo damage.

The more normal attacks you use, the more frequently he can activate a special Elemental Skill, or trigger a Charged Attack that doesn’t consume stamina. He can also rely on the Hexerei effect to trigger more instances of Elemental Skill, as well as Charged Attacks, making him a monster damage-dealer.

Varka, of course, has been a staple member of the cast, featuring in both the original story in a small cameo, as well as taking a bigger role in the recent Nod-Krai chapters. With the return to Mondstadt, his playable debut makes sense. His Story Quest will shed light on his encounter with the Wild Hunt, and the Great Wolf King of the North

The reruns for this version are going to be Flins — who will be available in the first phase of Event Wishes — as well as Skirk and Escoffier in the second phase. You can also look forward to the return of the Chronicled Wish with Mondstadt characters.

Staying on the theme of reminiscence, the big event in Luna 5 is centered around revisiting memories from the beginning of your time with Genshin Impact, and reuniting with old friends. In Echoes of Memory, you’ll witness familiar scenes that have been changed slightly, and you’ll need to use the Spotter Kamera to detect and record those differences.

The Knights of Favonius are hosting several other activities for everyone to take part in, including an event that lets you catch up with old friends over drinks which you make for them.

Outside of events, there’s a new set of Gliding and Combat Challenges. And, of course, there are new minigames that you can relax with. The Kamera is being utilised yet again, and this time you can use to capture sights from your time in spots across Natlan, Fontaine, and Sumeru. There’s also… a horde mode of a sort, where you fend off waves of enemies.

#4229. Remedy Explains Control Resonant's Most Memorable, Unexpected Sequence And Its [REDACTED] Inspirations

Please allow the first sentence here to warn you that this interview discusses a portion of Control Resonant that takes place near the end of the game and is arguably the most unexpected and surprising sequence. I encourage you to experience it without spoilers. So if you haven't beaten the game yet, please do, and then come back to this page.However, if you have beaten the game, or curiosity has driven you to learn what game has been redacted from the headline and why (it's the 1995 Super Nintendo RPG, EarthBound, by the way), then please read on.

In the late-game of Control Resonant – basically right before you tackle the final confrontation – the game suddenly shifts timeframe and genre to become a 16-bit RPG. The nostalgic lens turns the game into something that feels like 1995's EarthBound, complete with turn-based battles, in order to explain the trauma that Jesse and Dylan went through at a young age after they came across an object of power: the slide projector. The whole sequence is funny, heartbreaking, weird, and importantly effective at making you feel you are seeing a part of their past. It was particularly effective on me as I have fond memories of playing EarthBound and games like it when I was young. To see and experience Dylan and Jesse's childhood this way felt accurate, as absurd as that sounds.

I reached out to Remedy to specifically discuss that portion of the game. You can find the full e-mail interview below with the team members who contributed to its creation.

The big RPG backstory sequence for Jesse and Dylan – why approach the storytelling that way?

Lead level designer, Anne-Marie Grönroos: The basis for the whole sequence is that the Hedron attacks Dylan's mind, breaks his reality apart, and he has to rebuild himself. We wanted the reality-breaking part to affect the game itself and have the player feel some of the confusion Dylan is feeling by breaking the fourth wall.

Who pitched that sequence, how did they pitch it, and was it difficult to sell to the larger team?

Grönroos: At Remedy, ideas rarely come from a single person or team, and we rarely do formal pitches, but rather discuss and workshop ideas cross-craft until they start taking the shape of something we like. The initial idea from the writer was for this to be a text-based adventure, to return to a very early form of a video game to show that the Patterning is devolving him, but an Alan Wake 2 DLC had already done that, and we wanted to find something else.

Independently, some months ago a level designer had suggested a sidequest with JRPG pixel graphics, but that had gone nowhere. I remembered that and suggested doing an old Final Fantasy-style JRPG here, which also felt more fitting since that’s the type of game Dylan and Jesse would have played in their childhood, and not a text-based adventure. People got excited about that, and after some concerns about feasibility, we went forth with it. It helped that the level designer who had originally wanted to do the JRPG side quest is a big fan of these types of games and has made them before. I wouldn’t have dropped something this crazy on someone who wasn’t passionate about it and ready to figure out how to do it with our engine that’s not built for anything like this.

Is EarthBound (Mother in Japan) the primary inspiration for that sequence? Are there big fans of those games at Remedy?

Senior level designer in charge of the JRPG quest, Arhi Makkonen:The whole Quest was born from that childhood feeling I had when playing old JRPGs – Final Fantasy, Breath of Fire, Chrono Trigger, Secret of Mana, Bahamut Lagoon, and yes, Mother. The most important thing for me was capturing that feeling of a time when games felt like magic. I think many people can relate to that nostalgia, and now Jesse and Dylan share that feeling in the game.Visually, Mother was a major inspiration of course. Juuso Anttila is the concept artist who did all the splendid pixel art for Rebuild quest. Mother's style fits the mysterious Americana small town vibe perfectly. We also couldn't pass up the pun about a story revolving around "Not-Mother" that was made in the style of Mother.

Was it difficult to implement the sequence into the game? Did Remedy's Northlight Engine need significant work to account for the sequence?

Makkonen: The Northlight engine was designed to work perfectly for third-person action games. Well, Rebuild Quest is pretty much the opposite of that. Northlight is a specialized tool rather than a general-purpose one, so we had to come up with some rather creative solutions to create a 2D JRPG.

First of all, we’re faking the 2D look. In reality, the entire JRPG Ordinary exists within a 3D world that the camera simply views from directly overhead. It occupies a tiny patch in a remote corner of the game world—a space where 3D Dylan would barely have room to stand. The entire game-within-a-game is written in Lua; our incredibly versatile game designer, Tommi Saalasti, created the underlying system, upon which I was then able to build the story.

Since we didn't really have the tools to create a game like this, I had to hand-code every single detail. Dylan takes one step up, Dylan turns left (where Jesse hopefully is at that moment), text box 1, text box 2. The Lua script for the Rebuild quest alone probably contains as many lines of code as all the other quests in the game combined. And then there were things like animations were restricted to a maximum of two frames, and some UI elements were created using static particle effects.

So yes, we faced all sorts of challenges and compromises, but at the heart of it all was a wonderful story – simply told in a somewhat unconventional way. We trusted that the narrative would make up for some of the imperfections.

Remedy has a reputation for big unexpected and often crazy singular moments. What are the conversations like around delivering those? In pre-production, are there conversations like, "What is the big moment for this one?" Or do they happen pretty naturally?

Grönroos: They both happen naturally and we also have conversations about what the big moments should be. Sometimes we like a section so much that we decide to put even more resources and importance to it, even if it wasn’t supposed to be all that important from the get-go. The Into the Sinkhole quest, for instance, is a quest that wasn’t planned to be a “tentpole moment” from the start, but we kept putting more effort into it when it was shaping up to be something very special.

But most setpieces in the game were planned to be such from the early stages of pre-production. In Resonant, we wanted to have multiple standout moments instead of a single sequence like the Ashtray Maze overshadowing everything else, and I’m happy to see that players have different favorites.

And a different approach from Control is that several of these memorable moments (Sinkhole, Underpass Fault, the JRPG section) are more emotional and subdued instead of bombastic action (although we also have big action setpieces), which was an interesting challenge itself.

Was there a fear that the visuals would limit the emotional impact of the sequence?

Grönroos: Yes, but we decided to trust the writing. Several other games have managed to deliver a similar emotional impact despite pixel graphics (and sometimes because of them, since the level [of] abstraction can make characters more relatable and up to the player’s interpretation), so we weren’t too concerned.

Was there a fear that action game fans would be frustrated by the RPG sequence?

Grönroos: Yes, this was the main concern about the sequence. It was a very polarizing sequence in the playtests: people either loved or hated it. We did discuss shortening it significantly, but in the end decided to keep it as it is but added some fast travel options and make some parts skippable. There were more fans than haters, and we didn’t want to sacrifice something we really enjoyed.

How concerned were you about the actual RPG mechanics of that sequence?

Makkonen: Since Rebuild doesn't feature a vast number of battles, we didn't need to build particularly deep RPG or progression systems. The combat served as an additional storytelling tool – illustrating how bullies torment Dylan, showing his first fight (against rats, naturally), and depicting his eventual abduction by the FBC.

Refining the combat to be simple, yet offer the player meaningful choices required a few iterations. In addition to standard attacks, the children can occasionally use special abilities: Dylan delivers a heavy blow to a single enemy, while Jesse fires at everyone. Enemies deal enough damage that defending becomes necessary when multiple foes target the same character.

The lightbulbs in The Underpass mission goes in similarly unexpected, animated directions. How did that mission come about? What was the pitch like for that one?

Grönroos: That one started with the idea of doing something comically mundane, switching lightbulbs, and adding a paranatural twist to it. The cartoon man wasn’t in the initial version, but instead we were going to do live action videos and have Dylan get stuck in that video as the end twist. They were supposed to be old-fashioned “work safety” videos explaining how to change lightbulbs, and as the quest went on, it became more and more obvious that the maintenance guy in the videos was too aware of what Dylan was doing. This all came out from a one-hour workshop.

There wasn’t really a pitch, but rather a back-and-forth like “could we do a quest about Dylan changing lightbulbs in a ritualistic way? We could have these sentient work safety videos explain how to do it and “Dylan could get trapped inside the video.” Much later, when the live action turned out to be a no-go, we pivoted to the current cartoon instead, and that was even funnier than our initial idea.

#4228. 10 Soulslikes Where You’re Actually the Villain

Shane Limbaugh is a Contributor at DualShockers who began covering games professionally in 2025. A longtime gamer with a Bachelor’s Degree in Game Design and Criticism, Shane brings a design-focused perspective to his coverage, looking closely at how mechanics, systems, story, and player experience come together.

​Of all the genres in gaming, there isn’t one that stays as morally ambiguous as soulslikes. While the genre has grown to encompass a lot of different kinds of games, that question of morality remains the same.

Players are often a bit hesitant to become the villain of the story, but offering up that potential makes for a more difficult choice. Whether a player will embrace evil or remain on the path of good always makes for a good time.

This list consists of games that could be categorized as soulslike even if their main genre is a bit different. It does contain spoilers for certain endings, so you may want to read carefully to avoid anything you’d rather not know.

There are plenty of great shooters out there, but how about ones where you play the bad guy? Get ready for this edgy mix of dark adventures.

Hellpoint is an interesting soulslike game that sees players take on the role of a Spawn as they face off against all kinds of cosmic horrors. While trapped on a space station, players will make their way through boss encounters while making choices to determine their alignment.

You don’t have to play as the villain in Hellpoint, but you do have the option to align yourself with the Prodigal Spawn and perform a dark ritual. It is morally grey, but those choices do matter and can make players into the villain of their story.

In a genre that typically sticks to being morally grey, Death’s Gambit: Afterlife makes things a bit harder by making you an agent of death. In this Metroidvania soulslike, players will go up against immortals as they attempt to snuff out immortality altogether.

This one is tough because your motivations aren’t necessarily evil, but the results you achieve certainly make you a bit of a villain. By destroying immortality, you’ll be killing anything and everything connected to it, regardless of alignment.

You wouldn't typically imagine a game about giant robots digging so deep into the ambiguity of who a mercenary decides to fight for, but Armored Core VI does just that. The game is more of an action game than a soulslike, but with FromSoftware at the wheel, it still feels like one.

Playing as C4-621, you have a choice in who you help, and depending on your choice, a lot of things can happen. Despite the choice of endings, you do spend a lot of time fighting and killing the residents of Rubicon 3.

While it's fine playing the white knight trope, these JRPGs are ones where you play someone decidedly morally grey as a naughty anti-hero.

FromSoftware really enjoys giving players a choice in how they affect the world as a whole, and most of the time it's not for the better. Playing as an Ashen One, players will have to face off against the mighty Lords of Cinder and decide the fate of the world.

There is still that freedom of choice, but players can choose to simply burn the world themselves. This certainly makes you a villain to some, but it is still a choice, so it’s up to players if they become a villain.

As a Hunter in Bloodborne, your only purpose is to kill the monsters that plague the world and use their power to make yourself stronger. You may not start very villainous, but in the end you may become the very thing you set out to destroy.

In one of the endings, players can turn into a Great One, an otherworldly eldritch being that doesn’t follow our sense of morality. It could be up for debate whether this makes players the true villain, but it does seem a bit villainous to leave behind your humanity.

Elden Ring was a sensational game that expanded the soulslike genre into the open-world genre and gave players more freedom than ever before. With that freedom came plenty of choice, and those choices could end in disaster.

By taking the Frenzied Flame, players will cause a chain reaction of events that ends the game with the world on fire. The world may be a bit problematic, but causing mass destruction and burning the world to a crisp seems very villainous.

While playing as the protagonist, Wolf, players are given choices, some of which have long-standing consequences. The game isn’t a traditional soulslike, but with the difficulty and mechanics behind the game, it certainly feels like one.

Wolf is given a choice towards the back half of the game where he can either follow Iron Code or save Kuro. Following the code results in Wolf fully becoming a demon and killing many of the people he knows and cares about.

We like these games' heroes, but there's something about their villains that sticks with us.

The premise of the game seems to frame your character as the hero, but in true FromSoftware fashion, you can become the villain. Featuring a morality tracker, the more you kill innocents and do vile deeds, the closer you become to being Pure Black.

At the end of the game, players can decide to simply betray their allies up to that point, killing them and thrusting the world into a new age of darkness. Whether you were the villain throughout the game or not, at the end there’s no debating it.

Vampires are pretty much always the bad guys, although when it comes to Dr. Jonathan Reid, players can decide what happens. Whether he succumbs to the monster within or maintains some semblance of humanity is in the hands of players.

Whatever path the player takes determines what happens to London and its people. Leaning into the destructive nature of vampires leaves the city in complete collapse and causes the epidemic to continue unfettered.

Final Fantasy games as a whole have always been a bit out there in terms of story, but unlike the other games on this list, you are literally the villain. Playing as Jack along with the other Strangers as you attempt to stop Chaos from destroying the world.

By the end of the story, there’s only one option for our heroes, and that’s for Jack to embrace the Chaos and become the villain of the story. This sends him back in time and sets him up as Garland, the villain of the first Final Fantasy game.

A dark detective thriller where folklore is real, violence is chilling, and every choice has consequences.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#4227. Nioh 3 is, unsurprisingly, the fastest-selling game in the series with over a million units sold

Nioh 3 has taken the Nioh franchise to new heights, delivering its biggest-ever launch.

Even before the game came out, it was pretty easy to guess that Nioh 3 would be a hit. From the word of mouth leading up to launch, to the well-received free demo, there was little chance the action RPG wasn’t going to be a major deal.

Today, publisher Koei Tecmo has announced that the game has officially passed over one million copies sold worldwide across PC, and PlayStation 5. This makes it the fastest in the Nioh franchise to reach this milestone.

As a result of this fantastic launch, Nioh 3 has now pushed overall Nioh franchise sales to be over 10 million, which includes the original Nioh as well as Nioh 2. Today’s news comes just two weeks after the game arrived on PC, and PS5.

On Steam, where it’s available on PC, it shot up the Steam charts, and immediately broke the series’ previous best peak concurrent player count record. From there, the numbers kept growing, leading up to a stellar weekend where it peaked at 88,045 concurrent players on Steam, double that of its launch day.

This now stands as the largest for any Nioh game on Steam, and though we don’t have insight into how well it’s doing on PS5 specifically, it still shows that the Nioh series continues to grow.

Nioh 3 builds on everything the two prior games established, and pushes the series into the semi-open-world realm, with several larger maps that each cover a period of time in Japan’s history. In our Nioh 3 review we called it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.”

If you’re curious about the challenging and very rewarding action RPG, start with these gameplay tips, and don’t be shy to call upon a friend (or stranger) for help using our co-op guide.

#4224. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.
